name: Ādinātha
summary: Śiva as the first Nāth and first teacher of yoga; the Haṭhapradīpikā opens with homage to Śrī Ādinātha 'by whom the knowledge of haṭha yoga was taught' (HYP 1.1), and Nāth lineages begin with him. In Nāth accounts he taught Matsyendra, who overheard or received the teaching he gave to Pārvatī.

realization_account.text: The supreme Lord himself; the source of the teaching.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Matsyendranātha
summary: The first human Nāth after Ādinātha and guru of Gorakṣa; the Kaulajñānanirṇaya calls itself 'brought down' by Macchaghnapāda/Mīnapāda from Candradvīpa and tells how Bhairava as a fisherman recovered the scripture from a fish's belly (KJN 16). Nāth sagas tell how he forgot himself among the women of the Kadalī (or Strī) kingdom and was awakened by Gorakṣa. In the Kathmandu valley he is worshipped as Karuṇāmaya (Buṅga-dyaḥ, Rāto Macchindranāth), brought to end a drought caused by Gorakṣa; Tibetan tradition relates the name to the siddha Lūipa. Abhinavagupta praises 'Macchanda' as a Kaula master (Tantrāloka 1.7).

tradition.text: present in the four ages; Nāth hagiography

realization_account.text: Received the Kaula teaching from Bhairava/Ādinātha (in some Nāth tellings while in the form of a fish, overhearing Śiva teaching Pārvatī); fell into forgetfulness in the Kadalī kingdom and was re-awakened by his disciple Gorakṣa.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: HYP 1.5 lists both 'Matsyendra' and 'Mīna', and some traditions distinguish Mīnanātha from Matsyendra (e.g. as father/son); this shard keeps one entry and records the question in dsp:identity-of-matsyendra.

name: Gorakṣanātha
summary: Disciple of Matsyendra and the great organiser of the Nāth order, to whom the Nāths trace their panths, insignia and yoga; the Gorakṣaśataka, Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati, Amaraughaprabodha, Amaraughaśāsana and the Hindi Gorakh Bānī are ascribed to him. The tradition holds him immortal, appearing in every age; he rescues Matsyendra from the Kadalī kingdom, initiates Gopīcand, Bharthari and Pūraṇ Bhagat (Cauraṅgī), and in Vīraśaiva accounts meets Allama Prabhu. The Gorakhnāth Maṭh at Gorakhpur is his principal seat; Gorkha and the Gurkhas take their name from him.

tradition.text: immortal; appears in all four ages (tradition)

realization_account.text: Born by the power of Matsyendra's ash (vibhūti) — in the common north Indian and Marathi telling, the ash given to a childless woman was thrown on a dung-heap, and Matsyendra later called forth the boy from it; the Gorakṣaguṭikā gives a different origin. Perfected in body, deathless, master of all siddhis.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Jālandharanātha
summary: A siddha counted among the nine Nāths; in the Bengali Gopīcandra cycle he is Hāḍipā, the siddha living as a sweeper (hāḍi) who initiates King Gopīcandra at Mayanāmatī's request; his disciple is Kāṇha (Kānipā). Also in the Buddhist siddha lists as Jālandhari(pā).

realization_account.text: A great siddha whose power humbles kings; Gopīcandra's guru.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Kāṇha (Kānipā / Kānifnāth)
summary: U21 contribution: in Nāth tradition Kānipā/Kānupā is Jālandhara's disciple (Bengali saga) and, as Kānifnāth, one of the Marathi nine Nāths, with a samādhi shrine at Madhi (Ahilyanagar/Ahmednagar district). Whether this Nāth figure is the same as the Buddhist siddha Kāṇha / Kṛṣṇācārya is not settled.
notes: Registry id for the Buddhist mahāsiddha Kāṇha (U44). Identification with the Nāth Kānipā is the tradition's (shared siddha lists) and is disputed; HYP 1.7 'Kānerī' may or may not be the same figure.

name: Carpaṭanātha
summary: A Nāth siddha (Carpaṭi in HYP 1.6) to whom Hindi sayings are ascribed (Nāth Siddhoṁ kī Bāniyāṁ); in Chamba tradition the guru of the founder-king of Chamba; also named among alchemical siddhas; one of the Marathi nine Nāths (Carpaṭnāth).

name: Cauraṅgīnātha
summary: A Nāth siddha (Cauraṅgī in HYP 1.5): a prince whose hands and feet were cut off at a stepmother's false accusation and who was restored by the Nāth gurus — known in Punjab as Pūraṇ Bhagat and in Telugu as Sāraṅgadhara. The Prāṇ Saṅkalī is ascribed to him.

realization_account.text: Restored in body by the guru's grace after twelve years of practice (the tradition's story in its several versions).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Gahinīnātha
summary: Nāth guru of Nivṛttināth in the Marathi tradition, counted among the nine Nāths (the Marathi list); tradition places his meeting with Nivṛtti at the Brahmagiri near Tryambakeśvar and a samādhi at Gahinīnāthgaḍ.

name: Nivṛttināth
summary: Elder brother and guru of Jñāneśvar, initiated in the Nāth line by Gahinīnāth; Jñāneśvar calls himself 'Nivṛtti's servant' (nivṛttidāsu) throughout the Jñāneśvarī. Abhaṅgas are ascribed to him.
notes: Works field notes only that the Jñāneśvarī is dedicated to him; he is not its author.

name: Jñāneśvar
summary: U21 contribution: in the Nāth line through Nivṛttināth; the Jñāneśvarī names the Nāth sequence of teachers at its close and calls the swallowing of the body by the body the secret of the Nāth signal (6.291).

name: Bhartṛhari (Bharthari, the Nāth king-yogī)
summary: King of Ujjain in Nāth legend who renounced his throne — in the best-known telling after the fruit of immortality he gave his queen returned to him through her lover — and became a disciple of Gorakh; founder of the Bharthari (Vairāg) panth; hero of sung sagas; counted among the Marathi nine Nāths. Tradition often identifies him with the poet of the three śatakas and with Bhartṛhari the grammarian.
notes: Distinct id from tch:bhartrhari (the grammarian of the Vākyapadīya, U31). The tradition's identification of the three is not accepted by scholars.

name: Gopīcandra (Gopīcand)
summary: King of Bengal in the Nāth cycle, son of Mayanāmatī, who at his mother's insistence renounced his kingdom and queens and took initiation from Hāḍipā (Jālandhara) to escape an early death; hero of Bengali, Hindi and Rajasthani sagas.

name: Mayanāmatī
summary: Queen-mother in the Bengali Nāth cycle, a disciple of Gorakṣa who received the 'great knowledge' (mahājñāna) and with it power over death; she compels her son Gopīcandra to renounce. One of the few women siddhas of the Nāth tradition.

name: Revaṇanātha
summary: One of the Marathi nine Nāths (Revaṇnāth), held to be an incarnation of the Nārāyaṇa Camasa. In Karnataka the name Revaṇasiddha also belongs to a Vīraśaiva founder-figure; the relation between the two is unclear.

name: Nāganātha
summary: One of the Marathi nine Nāths (Nāgnāth / Nāgeśnāth), held to be an incarnation of the Nārāyaṇa Āvirhotra.

name: Dharmanātha
summary: Nāth yogī regarded as founder of the Dharamnāthī panth; tradition says he performed austerities on Dhinodhar hill in Kutch, where his seat remains.

name: Nityanātha
summary: Siddha named in the Haṭhapradīpikā's list (1.7); a Nityanātha is credited with alchemical and magical works (Rasaratnākara, Kāmaratna) and, in some manuscripts, with the Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati.
notes: Whether these are one person is uncertain.

name: Svātmārāma
summary: U21 contribution: author of the Haṭhapradīpikā, who bows to the Nātha guru and places himself after Matsyendra, Gorakṣa and the siddhas (HYP 1.2–9).

name: Bālnāth
summary: Nāth yogī associated with Tilla Jogian (Gorakh Ṭillā) in the Salt Range; in Wāris Shāh's Hīr he gives Rāñjhā the split-ear initiation.
notes: Distinct from the Himachali folk deity Bābā Bālaknāth (U59), with whom he is sometimes confused.

name: Mastnāth
summary: 18th-century Nāth yogī regarded as founder of the monastery at Asthal Bohar near Rohtak (Haryana).

name: Gambhīrnāth
summary: Nāth yogī of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh, Gorakhpur, revered as a realised yogī in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

name: Digvijaynāth
summary: Mahant of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh, Gorakhpur, in the mid-20th century.
notes: Listed only as a head of the Gorakhpur seat; succession Digvijaynāth → Avaidyanāth → Ādityanāth as commonly reported.

name: Avaidyanāth
summary: Mahant of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh, Gorakhpur, in the later 20th century.

name: Ādityanāth
summary: Present mahant of the Gorakhnāth Maṭh, Gorakhpur (from 2014), also a political figure.
notes: Recorded only as head of the seat; no teachings attributed.

name: Śekh Phayjullāh
summary: Bengali Muslim poet to whom the Gorakṣavijaya is ascribed.

name: Gauraṇa
summary: Telugu poet, author of the Navanāthacaritramu.

name: Dhuṇḍisuta Mālu (Narahari Mālu)
summary: Marathi author of the Navanātha Bhaktisāra.

name: Gūgā (Gogā, Jāhar Pīr)
summary: Warrior-saint of Rajasthan and Punjab, revered by Hindus and Muslims as a snake-protector; in the legend a disciple of Gorakhnāth, born through Gorakh's blessing to his mother Bāchal.

name: Ratannāth (Hājī Ratan)
summary: Nāth yogī remembered in Punjab and among Muslims of the north-west as Hājī Ratan; a centre of his cult was at Peshawar.

name: Dattātreya
summary: U21 contribution: in Marathi Nāth tradition Dattātreya instructs the Nāths (Navanātha Bhaktisāra) and appears with Gorakṣa (Gorakṣaguṭikā 1.24); Aghora regards him as ādiguru, who appeared to Kīnārām at Girnar and whose form was Bābā Kālūrām.

name: Kīnārām
summary: Founder of the present Aghora lineage at Krīm Kuṇḍ (Kīnārām Sthal), Varanasi. Tradition: born at Rāmgaṛh (Chandauli), he was first initiated by the Vaiṣṇava Śivarām, then received Aghora from Bābā Kālūrām, whom he recognised as Dattātreya (after a vision at Girnar); he wandered to Hiṅglāj and elsewhere, founded monasteries and wrote Hindi works — Vivekasār, Rāmgītā, Rāmrasāl, Gītāvalī.

realization_account.text: Received Aghora-dīkṣā from Kālūrām (Dattātreya); famed for miracles and for compassion to the poor; lived about 170 years.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Registry id. The dates are the tradition's; no independent confirmation checked.

name: Kālūrām
summary: Aghora ascetic of Varanasi, guru of Kīnārām, regarded in the tradition as Dattātreya himself; the Krīm Kuṇḍ seat is associated with him.

name: Śivarām (Kīnārām's Vaiṣṇava guru)
summary: Vaiṣṇava ascetic who gave Kīnārām his first initiation (tradition).

name: Bījārām
summary: Disciple and successor of Kīnārām at Krīm Kuṇḍ (tradition).
notes: The full succession list of Krīm Kuṇḍ heads is not reproduced (gap); only names recalled with some confidence are given.

name: Rājeśvar Rām
summary: 20th-century head (pīṭhādhīśvar) of Kīnārām Sthal, Krīm Kuṇḍ, Varanasi.

name: Siddhārth Gautam Rām
summary: Present head (pīṭhādhīśvar) of Kīnārām Sthal, Krīm Kuṇḍ, Varanasi (from 1978, as commonly reported), a disciple of Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām.

name: Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām
summary: Aghora teacher of Varanasi who founded the Śrī Sarveśvarī Samūh (1961) and a leprosy service ashram, taught Aghora as naturalness, service and the rejection of caste and social evils, and travelled abroad; he died in 1992.

name: Gurupad Sambhav Rām
summary: Disciple of Aghoreśvar Bhagavān Rām associated with the leadership of the Śrī Sarveśvarī Samūh.
